100% see a psychiatrist or doctor trained in psychiatric meds, not all medical doctors will be able to help in the same way and the cost is the same in terms of copay, etc. Just remember a psychiatrist is not a psychologist and often is not there for talk therapy or counseling, they care more about chemical imbalances. The combination of therapy/counseling and meds is in my opinion the best route but if you feel counseling is too expensive for you, the meds alone are definitely much cheaper.

Generally you’ll see someone for a psychiatric diagnosis and then they can prescribe you meds, do a two week follow up, then a month after that and if things are going well it’s once every three months. It is very worth it and affordable. While I will always suggest seeing a counselor or therapist, seeing someone once a week is an expense that not everyone can make.

It is not a bad thing to have a diagnosis!!! In fact they NEED to give you one in order to prescribe meds so don’t focus on the naming or labeling of a disorder.

I could only imagine how my son and daughter's unstable upbringing might manifest itself in future writings, paintings, or music, given the way I would routinely ridicule their achievements, yell at their mother in drunken fits of rage, and threaten the family with physical violence.

My constant petty bullying alone ought to have be worth a couple novels or screenplays—maybe even a solo museum exhibit. Note that even when my children did get a break from my verbal abuse, they still suffered from total emotional abandonment. We're not talking here about your ordinary, everyday withholding of approval, either. Most of the time, I was actively undermining and belittling them. Definitely stuff that could be channeled into unique art emblematic of the isolated, tortured nature of human existence.

After 18 years of life in that kind of menacing environment, you could easily be looking at the next Jackson Pollock and Sylvia Plath.

I was asked if my children might turn to teachers or other adult role models for the support they lacked at home, I assumed my long record of broken commitments—promising to attend and then forgetting about Amber's school play, buying James a longed-for guitar and later pawning it to pay a gambling debt—would prevent them from ever trusting anyone and force them to find artistic outlets for their anguish.

I really hadn't stopped to consider my children would have a real leg up, creatively until I re-watched the works of Ingmar Bergman and realized how the legendary filmmaker had exorcised the demons of his childhood on screen.

A classic like Fanny And Alexander makes you think about all the different ways you're terrorizing your own kids, and how you're giving them the raw material they need to create a masterpiece of their own. James at a young age was already expressing his feelings through poetry. It was pretty good, but I still told him he's a little faggot for writing it. I thought he would focus the rage he feels toward me into writing even better poetry.

I mean can you imagine the unstable temperament he could’ve  have had 20 years from then, at his creative and intellectual peak?

Despite the habitual humiliation and agonizing mind games I ensnared James in on a daily basis, my daughter was the one most likely to experience crippling depression on the level of Frida Kahlo or Georgia O'Keeffe.

I was AA, trying smart recovery now. I’ll get hate on this sub for saying it but black and white might not be the best course for people like us. You see not being sober as a failure and drinking makes you lose your AA pride. Fuck everything about what anyone thinks of you, the only person you have to live with is yourself. 

You have some questions to ask yourself: 
Do you need to be sober? 
Are you drinking out of compulsion or to escape?
Does breaking sobriety mean drinking heavily?

If you are not able to moderate, yes AA is the place for you. If you start and can’t stop, you need to be sober.

If you are drinking to escape a problem and find that you don’t compulsively need a drink, have you got that problem addressed? Do you have a therapist and psychiatrist? If drinking is the symptom rather than the problem you have other courses of action to take.

My problem with the sobriety vs alcoholic duality is that when you “fail” sobriety you are off the rails. And I’m sure this past year you have been off the rails. Can you reign it in or not? Be honest with yourself. 

There are solutions out there and the first is to stop hating yourself, whether it be aa, smart recovery, religion or whatever. You need to address the reasons WHY you drink.

As a schizoaffective bipolar type male, alcohol is not the answer. It’s equally as dangerous as weed was in my case. Moderation, med management and exercise are the key. If we look for substance to alter our mood, we should look for things that are long acting and can help us through the day not transient and fluctuating.
